Of course the ChatGPT dog cancer vaccine spawned a startup
Date: Wed Aug 12 08:09:34 2026 UTC-04:00

Remember that much-hyped story about an Australian tech entrepreneur using ChatGPT, Grok, and other AI tools to craft a personalized cancer vaccine for his dog? Well, surprise: He's launched a startup. 
That entrepreneur is Paul Conyngham, who says he is launching Gamgee to offer "personalised mRNA cancer vaccines for dogs." But his ambitions go well beyond dogs - and pets - with Gamgee's website promising the company will harness AI and genetics to develop personalized treatments for a range of diseases and species, including humans. 
At the center of Gamgee's origin story is Rosie, Conyngham's Staffordshire bull terrier-Shar Pei mix, who features prominently on Conyngham's social media and the startup's website, as well as its AI-generated anime launch video. When announcing Gamgee on X, Conyngham said "I used chatgpt + computational genomics to design a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine for her tumour. Several of her tumours shrank." 
Conyngham, who stresses on Gamgee's website that he is "not a biologist," credits that intervention with adding years to Rosie's life. Gamgee's stated mission is to do that at scale. In case the canine element is lost on its visitors, the website features a slideshow of adorable dogs alongside ages and purported cancer diagnosis to remind them "who we're building this for."
But as I reported for The Verge earlier this year, the science behind Rosie's story is considerably messier than Conyngham's neat account suggests. The exact role AI played in the endeavor wasn't clear, and researchers said the broad claims gave the technology too much credit while minimizing the role of the humans involved. Moreover, the protocol Rosie followed made it impossible to say whether the mRNA vaccine was responsible for her improvement, since it was administered alongside another therapy. 
That hasn't stopped the idea from attracting support. The startup is backed by storied tech incubator Y Combinator and says it is recruiting for its first clinical trials in Australia, with a waitlist open everywhere else (though Conyngham says they're "accepting cases globally."). On a section on its website aimed at veterinarians, Gamgee touts a roughly 75 percent tumor reduction in its "first documented case," while promising to require less than 20 minutes of a veterinarian's time, no new clinical workflows, and a finished "vaccine in hand" in around four weeks. The company cautions that this timeline is based on a single case and may vary. Costs aren't disclosed on the site. 
Gamgee says it's working in collaboration with the University of Queensland and institutes at the University of New South Wales in Australia, and Conyngham encourages potential funders or study partners to reach out. 
Ultimately, the company says its mission extends beyond dogs and other animals to personalized treatments for humans. For a startup built around a single dog whose improvement cannot be clearly attributed to the treatment at the core of its pitch, that's a grand ambition.

The vaccine, currently in clinical trials conducted by Mamula’s company TheraJan, targets protein families such as EGFR/HER2, which are responsible for tumor growth. By blocking these proteins and initiating a strong immune response that kills tumors, the vaccine has doubled 12-month survival rates when combined with standard treatments like surgery and chemotherapy—from 30–40% to 60–70%.

The vaccine gained attention following the remarkable recovery of Ranger, a golden retriever previously given little chance of survival. After receiving the vaccine, his cancer ceased progressing and disappeared from scans. Over 11 clinical trial sites across the U.S. are offering the treatment, free of charge, to eligible dogs. The vaccine is pending approval from the USDA and is expected to become the most affordable cancer treatment for dogs on the market. Given the prevalence of cancer in dogs—affecting one in four and half of those over age 10—the vaccine could have far-reaching impact. Mamula, inspired by the loss of his own dog, continues to receive grateful messages from pet owners whose dogs have benefited.
Yale-developed canine cancer vaccine shows promise for dogs, doubling survival rates
Date: Fri Aug  8 09:00:19 2025 UTC

NEW HAVEN - The owner of a 7-year-old golden retriever with an aggressive form of cancer was out of options.
Rick Kneisel, who lives alone in a small city south of Dayton, Ohio, first noticed an issue with his dog, Ranger, in March 2019. A noticeable limp that he initially thought was a pulled muscle turned out to be osteosarcoma, a common and fast-spreading bone cancer in dogs. For Kneisel, 75, the news was "devastating."
Ranger had one of his front legs amputated and endured months of treatment, including chemotherapy and an experimental drug from Ohio State University. But his condition worsened, Kneisel said. The cancer had spread to Ranger's lungs and his chances of survival were dimming.
That's when Kneisel called Dr. Mark Mamula, an immunologist and professor at the Yale School of Medicine, who, along with a team of researchers, were developing a canine cancer vaccine that's now changing the outlook for dogs with cancer and offering hope to their owners.

Why Dogs Now Play a Big Role in Human Cancer Research (https://www.wired.com/story/why-dogs-now-play-a-big-role-in-human-cancer-research)
【turn1048news23】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 7.3 years ago; Dogs are playing an increasingly significant role in cancer research due to their biological, genetic, and lifestyle similarities with humans. Through initiatives like the Cancer Moonshot, collaborative studies in comparative oncology are being boosted, focusing on promising areas such as immunotherapy. Dogs naturally develop cancers similar to humans, making them ideal candidates for studying complex tumor behaviors and testing treatments. Researchers have already used canine data to help develop human cancer drugs, including selinexor for multiple myeloma. Current Moonshot-related studies involve using genetically engineered viruses and immunotherapy combinations to combat cancers like canine lymphoma.

Dogs share environmental exposures with humans, enhancing their value in studying cancer development and treatment refinement. A groundbreaking trial, funded by the Open Philanthropy Project, is testing a universal cancer vaccine in 800 dogs, aiming to prevent tumors by training the immune system to recognize shared neoantigens. While results are pending, this large-scale trial offers invaluable insights and could pave the way for cancer prevention strategies in both dogs and humans. Participants benefit from regular veterinary checks and support for any cancer diagnosis, showcasing how canine companions might lead the way in transforming cancer prevention and treatment.
The Moonshot initiative also is funding unprecedented genomic sequencing of dogs, which will lead to a better understanding of cancer mutations and how they compare to the human version.
These projects all involve pets who acquired cancer naturally and who receive treatment through the studies, as humans often do. About half of dogs over the age of 10 will get cancer. "We are developing very critical, biologically rich information in patients who happen to be dogs," says Amy LeBlanc, a veterinarian and director of the National Cancer Institute's Comparative Oncology Program.
The cancer connection between dogs and humans goes beyond biology. "Dogs share all aspects of our environment," says veterinarian Diane Brown, who is CEO of the AKC Canine Health Foundation. "They drink the same water. They're on our same carpets, they're on our same grass. Of all pets, they are the ones who share our lives most fully."
The most audacious-and largest-ever-canine clinical trial is designed to prevent, not cure cancer. While it isn't funded by the Moonshot initiative, it carries a similar goal of leaping forward in cancer research.

Your Dog Is a Secret Weapon in the Fight Against Cancer (https://www.wired.com/story/dog-cancer-treatments)
【turn1048news24】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 3.4 years ago; Clinical trials involving dogs with cancer are revolutionizing cancer research and treatment for both animals and humans. The story of Jellybean, a Labrador retriever mix who defied odds after being diagnosed with metastatic osteosarcoma and participating in a trial at Tufts University, illustrates the potential of this approach. Despite an initial bleak prognosis, Jellybean responded remarkably to a combination of drugs, including a common blood pressure medication and experimental treatments, showing sustained remission of her tumors.

Canine cancers, particularly osteosarcoma, closely mirror human cancers in molecular and histologic makeup, making dogs valuable models for treatment studies. Dogs also provide practical advantages over traditional lab mice, such as natural cancer development, similar environmental exposures, and faster disease progression.

The research is part of a broader effort under the U.S. Cancer Moonshot initiative, which aims to cut cancer mortality rates by 50% over 25 years. Studies involving dogs are helping identify effective gene-drug interactions using machine learning, accelerating drug development and potentially lowering costs. Moreover, emerging trials explore immunotherapies and therapeutic vaccines originally tested in dogs for use in children with osteosarcoma. The ethical treatment of canine participants remains a top priority, highlighting their dual role as both patients and partners in medical progress.

The canine lymphoma blood test detects the levels of two biomarkers, the acute phase proteins (C-Reactive Protein and Haptoglobin). This test can be used for diagnostics, for screening, and for remission monitoring as well. We analyze clinical data, test various machine learning methods and select the best approach to these problems. Three family of methods, decision trees, kNN (including advanced and adaptive kNN) and probability density evaluation with radial basis functions, are used for classification and risk estimation. Several pre-processing approaches were implemented and compared. The best of them are used to create the diagnostic system. For the differential diagnosis the best solution gives the sensitivity and specificity of 83.5% and 77%, respectively (using three input features, CRP, Haptoglobin and standard clinical symptom). For the screening task, the decision tree method provides the best result, with sensitivity and specificity of 81.4% and >99%, respectively (using the same input features). If the clinical symptoms (Lymphadenopathy) are considered as unknown then a decision tree with CRP and Hapt only provides sensitivity 69% and specificity 83.5%. The lymphoma risk evaluation problem is formulated and solved. The best models are selected as the system for computational lymphoma diagnosis and evaluation the risk of lymphoma as well. These methods are implemented into a special web-accessed software and are applied to problem of monitoring dogs with lymphoma after treatment. It detects recurrence of lymphoma up to two months prior to the appearance of clinical signs. The risk map visualisation provides a friendly tool for explanatory data analysis.

Title: Smart Trial: Evaluating the Use of Large Language Models for Recruiting Clinical Trial Participants via Social Media
Authors: Xiaofan Zhou, Zisu Wang, Janice Krieger, Mohan Zalake, Lu Cheng
Date: Fri Sep 12 01:34:32 2025

Clinical trials (CT) are essential for advancing medical research and treatment, yet efficiently recruiting eligible participants -- each of whom must meet complex eligibility criteria -- remains a significant challenge. Traditional recruitment approaches, such as advertisements or electronic health record screening within hospitals, are often time-consuming and geographically constrained. This work addresses the recruitment challenge by leveraging the vast amount of health-related information individuals share on social media platforms. With the emergence of powerful large language models (LLMs) capable of sophisticated text understanding, we pose the central research question: Can LLM-driven tools facilitate CT recruitment by identifying potential participants through their engagement on social media? To investigate this question, we introduce TRIALQA, a novel dataset comprising two social media collections from the subreddits on colon cancer and prostate cancer. Using eligibility criteria from public real-world CTs, experienced annotators are hired to annotate TRIALQA to indicate (1) whether a social media user meets a given eligibility criterion and (2) the user's stated reasons for interest in participating in CT. We benchmark seven widely used LLMs on these two prediction tasks, employing six distinct training and inference strategies. Our extensive experiments reveal that, while LLMs show considerable promise, they still face challenges in performing the complex, multi-hop reasoning needed to accurately assess eligibility criteria.

Matching cancer patients to clinical trials is essential for advancing treatment and patient care. However, the inconsistent format of medical free text documents and complex trial eligibility criteria make this process extremely challenging and time-consuming for physicians. We investigated whether the entire trial matching process - from identifying relevant trials among 105,600 oncology-related clinical trials on clinicaltrials.gov to generating criterion-level eligibility matches - could be automated using Large Language Models (LLMs). Using GPT-4o and a set of 51 synthetic Electronic Health Records (EHRs), we demonstrate that our approach identifies relevant candidate trials in 93.3% of cases and achieves a preliminary accuracy of 88.0% when matching patient-level information at the criterion level against a baseline defined by human experts. Utilizing LLM feedback reveals that 39.3% criteria that were initially considered incorrect are either ambiguous or inaccurately annotated, leading to a total model accuracy of 92.7% after refining our human baseline. In summary, we present an end-to-end pipeline for clinical trial matching using LLMs, demonstrating high precision in screening and matching trials to individual patients, even outperforming the performance of qualified medical doctors. Our fully end-to-end pipeline can operate autonomously or with human supervision and is not restricted to oncology, offering a scalable solution for enhancing patient-trial matching in real-world settings.

Automatic identification of clinical trials for which a patient is eligible is complicated by the fact that trial eligibility is stated in natural language. A potential solution to this problem is to employ text classification methods for common types of eligibility criteria. In this study, we focus on seven common exclusion criteria in cancer trials: prior malignancy, human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, psychiatric illness, drug/substance abuse, and autoimmune illness. Our dataset consists of 764 phase III cancer trials with these exclusions annotated at the trial level. We experiment with common transformer models as well as a new pre-trained clinical trial BERT model. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of automatically classifying common exclusion criteria. Additionally, we demonstrate the value of a pre-trained language model specifically for clinical trials, which yields the highest average performance across all criteria.
